name: Progress Street
description: A heartfelt, 1980s-inspired AOR and stadium synth-rock album from The Stardust Engine, recorded in 2004 at their home on Progress Street NE in Blacksburg, Virginia. Making the full-blooded 1980s melodic rock record that Apex Records never let them make in 1987, Progress Street celebrates collegiate roots, upright pianos, second-hand 1984 synthesizers, and unbreakable family unity—immortalized on the cover alongside the band's brand-new custom 2004 Prairie Coachworks RLFD30 low-floor shuttle coach before exhaustion forced them into their Burnout Hiatus.
subtitle: The 2004 Blacksburg Homecoming Album (Final Release Before the Burnout Hiatus)
linerNotes: After the sprawling, emotionally exhausting double-album ambition of the 2003 Twin Moons project (Sanctuary Zero-G and Mile Marker 98), the five members of The Stardust Engine didn't book a commercial studio in Los Angeles or London. Instead, they went home to Progress Street NE in Blacksburg, Virginia.

Setting up their gear in the living room where it all began in 1985, Ryan, Cassidy, Evan, Tyler, and Holly made a pact: they were going to record the full-blooded, uncompromised 1980s Album-Oriented Rock (AOR) and stadium synth-rock record that Apex Records never let them make in 1987.

Progress Street is a love letter to their collegiate roots at Commonwealth Polytechnic Institute (CPI), to Cassidy's childhood upright piano and second-hand 1984 analog polyphonic synthesizer, to Saturday nights shaking the earth at The Crucible, and to riding Blue Ridge Transit's Route 1 home in the rain. Yet beneath the soaring hooks and triumphant stadium choruses, the album captures a band running on absolute fumes—culminating in a heartfelt final track where they promised their fans they were staying together as a family, right before pulling the plug and entering their decade-long Burnout Hiatus (2004–2014).

studioArchives.title: The Cover Art: Unit 1985 on Progress Street NE
studioArchives.content: The album cover was photographed at dusk on Progress Street NE right outside the family house. Parked at the curb is the band's brand-new custom 2004 Prairie Coachworks RLFD30—a 30-foot Restyled Low-Floor diesel shuttle bus finished in Obsidian Midnight with a cosmic nebula wrap, front-door-only boarding, a deployed aluminum ADA wheelchair ramp, and glowing amber Luminator LED signs reading PROGRESS STREET and THE STARDUST ENGINE. Because Holly, Evan, and Tyler all held Class A Commercial Driver's Licenses (CDLs) with Passenger and Airbrake endorsements, the family drove their own bus without hiring outside drivers.

studioArchives.title: The Sound of Exhaustion & The Burnout Hiatus
studioArchives.content: Delivering three massive studio albums in less than eighteen months (Sanctuary Zero-G, Mile Marker 98, and Progress Street) while running Engine Room Records pushed Ryan's physical stamina and Cassidy's sensory bandwidth past the redline. Tracks like "Running on Redline", the resurrected full-band AOR arrangement of "Empty Arenas", and the closing farewell "Last Bus Home: Lights Out on Progress Street" were written as a deliberate, loving sign-off so Forger Nation knew the family was intact even as the stage lights went dark until 2015.

studioArchives.title: Narrative Crossover: "Before the Distance: The Story of John & Erin"
studioArchives.content: The songs of Progress Street (especially "Route 1: Midnight Headlights", "Fifth Gear: The Architect's Shield", and "Before the Distance") and the 1990 acoustic demos later unearthed on Lost Sounds (2007) form the emotional backbone of the 2004 Blacksburg novel Before the Distance: The Story of John & Erin—where fraternal twins John and Erin (portrayed by Ryan and Cassidy) fight for survival and autonomy two blocks from Commonwealth Mall on Progress Street NE.
